q: Some physical quantities of physics are completely described by a single number (or magnitude) with an appropriate unit.
e: True. Some physical quantities of physics are completely described by a single number (or magnitude) with an appropriate unit. With an appropriate unit is an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: Quantities that have only magnitude are called vector quantities.
e: False. Quantities that have both magnitude and direction are called vectors. This claim used only vector quantities in place of both and direction vectors.

q: Quantities that have both magnitude and direction are called vectors.
e: True. Quantities that have both magnitude and direction are called vectors. Every quantity named in that sentence is being used in its physics sense.

q: The length of a ship being 30 m is an example of a vector quantity.
e: False. The mass of a block being 500 g is an example of a scalar quantity. A scalar is done once you have the size and the unit.

q: The mass of a block being 500 g is an example of a scalar quantity.
e: True. The mass of a block being 500 g is an example of a scalar quantity. A scalar is done once you have the size and the unit.

q: A plane flying with a velocity of 20 mi h⁻¹ towards east is an example of a vector quantity.
e: True. A plane flying with a velocity of 20 mi h⁻¹ towards east is an example of a vector quantity. Velocity is directed. Speed is the size of that velocity.

q: A force acting on a body being 20 N upwards is an example of a scalar quantity.
e: False. The mass of a block being 500 g is an example of a scalar quantity. A scalar is done once you have the size and the unit. Force here means a push or pull that can change a body's state of motion.

q: In printing, vectors are represented by boldface type, such as $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{v}$, $\mathbf{s}$.
e: True. In printing, vectors are represented by boldface type, such as $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{v}$, $\mathbf{s}$. Every quantity named in that sentence is being used in its physics sense.

q: In handwriting, vectors are indicated by placing arrows on the bottom of their symbols.
e: False. In handwriting you put the arrow on top of the vector symbol, not underneath. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$ means $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal in magnitude and have the same direction.
e: True. The vector relation $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$ means $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal in magnitude and have the same direction. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ means $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal in magnitude but have opposite directions.
e: True. The vector relation $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ means $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal in magnitude but have opposite directions. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = 2\vec{B}$ means the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is two times the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ and the direction of $\vec{A}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{B}$.
e: False. The vector relation $\vec{A} = -3\vec{B}$ means the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is three times the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ and the direction of $\vec{A}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{B}$. This claim used 2\vec{B}$ two in place of -3\vec{B}$ three.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = -3\vec{B}$ means the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is three times the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ and the direction of $\vec{A}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{B}$.
e: True. The vector relation $\vec{A} = -3\vec{B}$ means the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is three times the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ and the direction of $\vec{A}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{B}$. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: Using graphical method, a vector may be represented by an arrow.
e: True. Using graphical method, a vector may be represented by an arrow. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The length of the arrow representing a vector is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the vector.
e: False. The drawn arrow is longer when the vector is larger. Length is directly proportional to magnitude. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: To add $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, first draw $\vec{A}$, then draw $\vec{B}$ such that the tail of $\vec{B}$ is at the tip of $\vec{A}$.
e: True. To add $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, first draw $\vec{A}$, then draw $\vec{B}$ such that the tail of $\vec{B}$ is at the tip of $\vec{A}$. Every quantity named in that sentence is being used in its physics sense.

q: The vector sum $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$ is called the resultant vector.
e: True. The vector sum $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$ is called the resultant vector. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The resultant vector is drawn from the tip of $\vec{A}$ to the tail of $\vec{B}$.
e: False. The resultant runs from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the last one, not from tip back to tail. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: Vector addition is commutative, so $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$.
e: True. Vector addition is commutative, so $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: In algebraic notation, $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$.
e: True. In algebraic notation, $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$. Every quantity named in that sentence is being used in its physics sense.

q: To subtract $\vec{B}$ from $\vec{A}$, we add $\vec{A}$ and a vector with the same magnitude as $\vec{B}$ but its direction is the same as that of $\vec{B}$.
e: False. To subtract B you add a vector of the same size as B but opposite in direction. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: Vector subtraction is commutative.
e: False. Vector subtraction is not commutative. Swap the order and the result reverses. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The process of sub-dividing a vector into two or more vectors is called resolution of a vector.
e: True. The process of sub-dividing a vector into two or more vectors is called resolution of a vector. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The new vectors obtained from resolution are called vector components of the original vector.
e: True. The new vectors obtained from resolution are called vector components of the original vector. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: A useful application of vector resolution is sub-dividing a vector into two perpendicular components, namely, horizontal component and vertical component.
e: True. A useful application of vector resolution is sub-dividing a vector into two perpendicular components, namely, horizontal component and vertical component. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.

q: The x-component of a vector $\vec{A}$ inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the x-axis is $A_x = A \sin \theta$.
e: False. The y-component of a vector $\vec{A}$ inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the x-axis is $A_y = A \sin \theta$. This claim used x-component $A_x in place of y-component $A_y.

q: The y-component of a vector $\vec{A}$ inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the x-axis is $A_y = A \sin \theta$.
e: True. The y-component of a vector $\vec{A}$ inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the x-axis is $A_y = A \sin \theta$. A vector is not finished until you also say the direction.
